Dark Souls 1 is a masterpiece. I went into this expecting an outdated jankfest but instead got a well-crafted and sadistically challenging experience that tested me and my sanity in ways most modern Soulslikes haven’t—even those made by FromSoft.

My first few sessions all ended in rage quits, and I don't recall having said this many gamer words ever since I quit League of Legends almost a decade ago.

[hr][/hr]
[h1]Difficulty[/h1]
Dark Souls 1 has been referred to by many as “easy”—especially compared to something like Sekiro—with the implication that with difficulty comes quality. After having experienced this masterpiece, I can confidently say that this notion of Dark Souls 1 being easy comes from a fundamental misunderstanding of difficulty.

What is difficulty? What decides whether something is a challenge or a cakewalk? I’d suggest it to be the amount of effort and thinking a player has to put in to overcome the challenges set forth by the developers. Part of the draw of games with high difficulty is that, the greater the challenge faced, the greater the satisfaction received when we finally overcome it.

And when we talk about “difficulty” in Soulslikes, the conversation seems to be focused solely on how hard the bosses are. It’s always Malenia this, Malenia that, Waterfowl this, Waterfowl that.

However, a large part of the difficulty in Dark Souls 1 is focused on the maps themselves: the valleys, forests, caves, catacombs, and dungeons you’d have to work through to finally arrive at the boss at the end.

You are presented with numerous challenges that you can’t solve with a simple well-timed dodge roll—challenges that are less about trying to figure out how to dodge Waterfowl Dance and more about keeping your wits about you as you explore this vast and beautiful world.

[h1]Exploration[/h1]
The map design in Dark Souls 1 is a work of art. Unlike in more modern Soulslikes, the way forward isn’t always clear—you are forced to trawl through the unknown until you finally happen upon your destination.

You have classic ganks, ambushes behind corners, and archers shooting at you from seemingly unreachable places. However, accompanying them is a deluge of sadistic map design choices seemingly intended to engender a rage-filled, “ARE YOU FUCKING SERIOUS?!” every time you encounter one.

Later game areas also often feature certain cancerous mechanics that would probably have driven me insane had I not acclimated to and embraced the BS with a simple, “Oh, so we’re doing this now? Ahaha, okay, let’s go.”

What’s more, hidden paths flanked by perilous drops that would lead to secret areas in other games are, in fact, often the intended path in Dark Souls 1. As someone who always takes the time to clear the entire area of enemies before exploring every inch of the map, I [u]adore[/u] this map design.

It is often unclear whether the path I’m taking would lead to yet another secret area or the boss, and this sense of uncertainty is so much more mysterious and fun than when the Site of Grace is literally pointing to the next one. It’s also really nice how the fog gates here don’t always lead to bosses, which makes the surprise when you finally find a boss even greater.

[b][u]NPCs[/u][/b]
Some NPCs give you major hints about how to proceed or how your actions would influence the world, which is really cool. I had to retrain myself to actually pay attention to NPCs again due to how often modern games’ NPCs just spew pointless nonsense.

However, certain NPCs should really, REALLY repeat their vitally important hints, because they are the ONLY indicators for how to proceed. If any hint was needed for this game, it would be to [b][u]listen very carefully to what the first NPC you meet at the hub tells you[/u][/b]. Write it down or screenshot it if you have to.

[b][u]Rewards[/u][/b]
What about your reward for finally overcoming these challenges? In other games, your reward for clearing some dumb puzzle is usually a useless ring the devs placed there for the sole sake of being a “reward”.

In Dark Souls 1, you get anything from the emotional release of finally clearing the area, to secret paths leading to Bonfires and NPCs, to even one where you’re able to (moderate early-game spoilers) [spoiler]kill some bastard who would otherwise shoot at you with magic for 80% of the entire boss arena[/spoiler]. This is the most fun I’ve had with exploration in a very long time.

Now, this is not always perfect—I personally hate illusory walls because the ways to discover them are either a) unreasonably long periods of rolling into and hitting walls or b) using guides, both of which are extremely anti-fun. While this game hints at some of them, many are insanely hidden and often lead to extremely important NPCs and areas.

[b][u]Do Not Use Guides[/u][/b]
The last thing I will say about this topic is to never look up anything unless you’re absolutely, definitely, 100% stuck. And unless you want this game to become a boring cakewalk, do not look up an area or progression guide. A lot of the difficulty in this game is about exploring the unknown and figuring out how best to proceed. You can face that challenge head on—or you can Fextralife the fun out of the game.

You are ultimately free to do whatever you want, but I will tell you that using a guide for this masterpiece of a game is like flipping on a switch for Elden Ring that will summon a Mimic Tear +10 at the start of every major fight—a switch you can never turn off.

Embrace the unknown. Get lost, get mad, and git gud.

[h1]Boss Fights[/h1]
Compared to more modern Soulslikes, the difficulty in many boss fights comes less from the bosses’ movesets themselves and more from the arenas in which said fights take place.

I won’t spoil anything, but I will stress that instead of solely testing your reaction speed and the dexterity of your fingers to dodge through attacks, the test of skill here is often about forcing the player to figure out ways to mitigate the sadistic and annoying cancer present in many of the boss fights.

The collection of bosses in Dark Souls 1 is such a perfect blend of testing your brain along with your skill. While I definitely enjoy my Waterfowl Dancing amputees and old men armed with katana, spear, and Glock, this style of difficulty is so much more varied and enjoyable, even if the fights themselves are indeed easier from a skill-based perspective.

[b][u]Runbacks[/u][/b]
While the runbacks here are definitely longer than those in modern Soulslikes, I didn’t feel as annoyed for some reason.

Since the difficulty in modern Soulslikes is concentrated almost solely in the bosses, runbacks in those games feel like a nuisance. In contrast, since the difficulty in Dark Souls 1 seems more puzzle-focused, doing the runbacks quickly, safely, and efficiently felt like simply yet another puzzle to be solved.

Or maybe I’m just glazing because I still can’t believe how good this game is.

[h1]Final Words[/h1]
If you love Soulslikes, you owe it to yourself to try this game. Take a couple of hours to get used to the jank, turn off the Google Search, and give yourself over to the cancerous, sadistic masterpiece awaiting you.

First of all, the reason you're seeing so many negative reviews is that Bandai Namco in their infinite wisdom decided to release what was essentially a bugfix update as a separate $40 game. 

The owners of the old PC port were given 50% off discount coupons but $25 was still way too much for the improvements that were already mostly available through fan fixes and mods. This essentially split the player base in two as both versions of the game have separate online. To be fair, the old PC port, Prepare To Die Edition, was extremely low effort. It was locked at the internal resolution of 1024x720 (same as on the PS3 and 360), only 30 fps, very poor keyboard & mouse support, no anti-cheat system of any kind.

The improvements in Dark Souls: Remastered include:
- Any resolution support, 1080p, 4K etc.
- 60 fps (locked and tied to game speed).
- Full keyboard & mouse support including button prompts.
- A more advanced soft lighting system.
- A more advanced particle system (dust, fire, fog etc effects).
- Optimized for multi-core systems, so no random lag spikes like in the original.
- Full HD UI/HUD, including HUD scaling (from 60% to 100%).
- The worst of the textures have been redrawn at higher resolutions.
- A better matchmaking system that checks for gear not just level.
- A rigorous anti-cheat system.
- Some bug fixes, e.g. the "dead angle" exploit in PvP.
- Various quality of life improvements, e.g. being able to change covenants at bonfires, use multiple consumables all at once, an extra bonfire in a certain area etc.

The old PC port was de-listed and you can't buy it anymore (unless you look for scalpers that sell the remaining keys for $100+). Not that there's any reason to, Remastered is where it's at.

Now about the game itself. It's the OG Dark Souls. You're probably thinking, is it hard? Both yes and no. The difficulty mostly comes from the game having absolutely no hand-holding. 
The world is designed metroidvania style, but there's no map. 
The game has a plethora of possible character builds and gameplay mechanics, but nobody will tell you what is safe to invest in. 
You might spread your points too thin and end up with a worthless build that will make the game much harder than it needs to be. Or you might accidentally kill (or fail to save) an important NPC and end up missing out on a powerful weapon/spell/upgrade. Even if you realize you messed up it might be too late because there's only one save slot per character, so every decision is final and permanent. 
There's minimal dialog and the "tutorial" is just explaining what each button does.

In my opinion, these design choices were made to create a sense of community. You're supposed to learn from other players how to progress though the game. At bare minimum, read up on the basic builds, such as STR, DEX and "quality" (combined STR/DEX) builds. 
Feel free to spice up your build with some magic, but don't go for a pure caster, they require meta knowledge to be viable. 

Be patient, don't fight more than one opponent at a time, block their attacks with your shield and wait for openings. 

The game rewards a careful approach. If an area is proving to be too hard, then try going elsewhere. Or stick with it, there's often a good reward for tackling a difficult location early on.

As long as your build is sound and you're not playing too recklessly you shouldn't have too hard of a time with the game.
I played a typical STR 27/DEX 40 quality build with sword and board and beat all bosses with only a few retries, and some of them (especially mid-game) I took out on my first try. 

Keep your encumbrance under 25% (or at least 50%) load and you will move much faster and be able to circle strafe around the bosses and get a lot of easy hits in during their attack animations.

Overall, I highly recommend you grab DS:R if you enjoyed the first, or are looking to get your feet wet, the improvements are worth it.

Dark Souls 1 has always been the black sheep of this series when it comes to the quality of the PC release, so when Namco announced that they are partnering with QLOC to remaster it, I was very excited to finally be able to play the game without tons of fan-made mods to fix the problematic issues.
Unfortunately I was severely let down. 
But let's break it down, shall we?

[b][h1]PROS:[/h1][/b]
- Consistent 60 FPS

[b][h1]CONS:[/h1][/b]
- There's no significant graphics improvement. We are talking about a game that's 6 years old! 
Updating the graphics quality with today's technology should have been prioritized. 
Take a look at how much Scholar of the First Sin improved in terms of visuals compared to Dark Souls 2, despite being released only a year(!) later, and then compare Dark Souls 1 Remastered to the original release.
- Izalith still looks horrible! If there's one zone that could have used the polish, then it's Izalith!
- The delay on PC controls is still not fixed. Yes, I played all Souls titles with keyboard/mouse settings and all titles were perfectly playable, except for Dark Souls 1. One of the point of this Remastered version was supposed to be ironing out the control issues!
- Menu navigation is still as atrocious as I remember
- Arrow hitboxes are still inaccurate. Projectiles will get stuck in invisible walls!

Last but not least, the main reason I'm giving this a thumbs down is because the Remastered Edition was handled by QLOC. QLOC is a well-known localization company with an excellent track record of helming the ports for titles such as Dragon's Dogma, Tales of Zestiria or the Dragon Ball Xenoverse series. All of which are excellent, quality PC releases.
So the fact that they are responsible for something as lazy as Dark Souls: Remastered is rather insulting.

While the game only cost only 20€ I just can't justify giving out money for a lazy effort as this. Hence the refund.

If classic video games have equivalents in the realm of literature, I'd argue that "Dark Souls" is video gaming's very own "Paradise Lost" or "Divine Comedy." It's basically a big, brilliant, video game rendering of hell. Not so much in its setting, although it is set in a land populated by undead, but more so in its game mechanics. “Dark Souls” is a game all about suffering in the pursuit of perpetually unfulfilled and unfulfillable desires. Such an approach to gameplay certainly isn’t new to video games. Many MMO’s have made an endless progression of “carrots on a stick” into a business model. What’s unique about “Dark Souls,” however, is its hostility to the player in obtaining these carrots. It goes out of its way to make sure that players suffer in pursuit of the desire to beat the next boss, get the better armor, or level up one more time. Not only will you die and die repeatedly, but once you accomplish one desire, there’s always something new to replace it (another boss! another set of armor! higher stats!, New Game +!, New Game ++!, etc, etc, etc). Indeed, upon completing the game, in the “good” ending your avatar’s body is burned off into nothingness, perhaps being freed from its perpetual cycles of unfulfillable desire, yet you yourself are spit right back into the start of the game, repeating everything once more only with harder enemies and the devious promise of greater rewards.

The conception of hell as being existence dominated by perpetually repeating cycles of unfullfillable desire probably has more relationship to eastern religious traditions than western (no surprise that the game is Japanese). In other words, in its gameplay mechanics, it could be argued that “Dark Souls” is basically “Paradise Lost: Buddhist edition.” There are western analogies too, though. CS Lewis outlined a similar conception of hell from a Christian perspective in "The Great Divorce," arguing that hell is ultimately nothing more than a mindset characterized by endlessly and obsessively repeated cycles of thought. And for the atheists among us, Sartre's "No Exit" might be another literary analogy, not only because Sartre defined human existence as the mind’s impossible desire to be both being “in itself” and “for itself” at once, but also because the ability for players in "Dark Souls" to "invade" your single player game and kill you at inopportune times makes the famous statement in "No Exit" that "hell is other people" completely apt.

In case it isn't clear, though, saying that playing “Dark Souls” is like being in hell is maybe one of the nicest things I’ve ever said about a game. "Dark Souls" is not just one of the leanest, meanest, and best ARPGS I've ever played, but one of the best video games I've played, period. It’s a game where everything it has to say is reduced entirely to the language of its own game mechanics. It’s not trying to tell a story, or create compelling characters, or be a movie or a book. It’s simply a game and any meaning that you could potentially derive from this comes almost entirely from its status as a game. This makes it, if not one of the best RPGs ever, definitely the most honest. It's just simple, unadorned, brilliantly designed, and entirely compelling gameplay. An RPG boiled down to its absolute essence of dying, developing combat skills, and dying again in the endless pursuit of more loot and more power. The lack of trappings such as plot or character that might distract from what it actually is, gives the game the odd and entirely unique effect of deconstructing itself as you play it. You quickly realize that any goal you obtain will inevitably be replaced by another goal that’s further away, so you actively start to question the point of pursuing those goals; in the same heartbeat that you willingly spend 2 more hours grinding souls for armor that you don’t need (because it will raise my physical defense stats by 5 points, damn it, so I have to have it!). No game has made me question my own motives and reasons for playing it, and, indeed, actively dared me not to play it, more than “Dark Souls.” Which I think is kind of brilliant in its way. “Dark Soul’s” ultimate lesson, if it has one, is that in games, as in life, the only way to truly beat the “hellish” cycle of perpetual desire is to quit playing entirely.

Second, Dark Souls for PC is *still* buggy, even in this iteration. This isn't a hardware problem. My computer runs games like The Witcher 3 butter-smooth, even at preposterously high graphical settings. I can decorate Fallout: New Vegas with enough mods to turn it into something like a digital Christmas tree. Dark Souls III sails along at 60 FPS without exception. But no matter which settings I run Remastered at -- even at the very lowest settings possible! -- it consistently has a severe stuttering problem. At times, even to the point of unplayability. For those of you keeping score at home, this is actually a step *down* from what the Prepare to Die edition offered. I'm told this issue has surfaced for many after a patch, ironically enough. Were it any other game, I'd advise you to wait until another patch came out to rectify the issue, but as many of us are already aware, From Software are far from unwilling to send you products that are perpetually broken to some extent. I'd love it if they fixed this, but I don't believe it's something we can take for granted from this company.

Finally, the quality of life upgrades here wouldn't warrant a $20 price tag for an upgrade, even presupposing the game worked for you. The modding community has already taken steps to resolve the Prepare to Die edition's shortcomings -- DSFix and DSMFix, for instance. They've even created visual mods to make the game look much lovelier than Remastered does. These mods are free, which, rounding up, is about infinitely better than $20.  

In brief: if you already have Prepare to Die, stick to that. If you're looking to get Dark Souls for the first time, consider purchasing it for your console, if you have one.

Dark Souls: A Beautifully Brutal Lesson in Self-Hate

Dark Souls isn’t just a game — it’s an experience. Specifically, the experience of being repeatedly and unapologetically bullied by medieval architecture, undead warriors, and the very concept of hope.

You don’t play Dark Souls. You survive it. Barely. Then you die. Then you survive a bit more. Then you roll off a cliff because your fat-fingered dodge was two pixels off. Classic.

The story? Oh, it's there. Somewhere. Probably scribbled on a wall behind a hidden wall behind another hidden wall guarded by a depressed dragon. Every NPC speaks in riddles, metaphors, or what sounds like Shakespeare having an existential breakdown. Meanwhile, you’re standing there in a rusty bucket-helmet, covered in regret and moss.

Combat is tight, rewarding, and feels great — for the five seconds before a 12-foot skeleton dropkicks you into the sun. Boss fights are majestic duels where you die in 0.3 seconds, whisper “okay, fair,” and queue up to die again.

And let’s talk about mimics. Remember how other games reward curiosity? Not here. In Dark Souls, opening the wrong chest gets you eaten alive by a demonic tongue monster. Trust no one. Especially furniture.

The game’s world design is stunning in a “look how beautiful this place is, shame it wants me dead” sort of way. You’ll traverse haunted castles, poison swamps, and hell dimensions… all while questioning your life choices and the sanity of the developers.

Final Verdict: 9/10

Recommended for people who think “fun” is overrated and want to feel something. Anything.

Let's begin by adressing the cheating issue. In my original review I said "Cheaters are already infesting the game and getting legitimate players banned from online through invasions.". Now upon further examination of the issue it seems I may have been following a wave of misinformation. Let me explain. Yes, there are cheaters. They are invading players and killing them instantly, putting various crippling debuffs on them and breaking their equipment. Apparently there are ways to back up your save file regularly to help deal with this issue. Obviously that is a bit of a hassle and should not be required but it is something that you can do. 

Now the real question. Are they getting legitimate players banned from participating online? The answer is... Yes and maybe not? Yes, because you can definitely get softbanned if you pick up a modified item dropped by someone else such as armor and weapons with impossible upgrades. Maybe not, because apparently there is no good evidence of people being softbanned for being killed by a cheater. Bottom line, always be careful about picking up items dropped by other players and back up your save files regularly if you want to play online without the risk of having your character messed up. I can't 100% guarantee that this is enough to keep your character safe but given the limited information that has been gathered it seems like the best course of action at the moment if you want to play online. 

By the way, you might be wondering what a softban is. Basically, your game is messed up in a way that the anticheat is able to detect and it prevents you from matching up with the general playerbase and instead only lets you play with other people who have been caught by this system. It is usually not clear when this occurs to you which is why it is hard to provide evidence for how and when this happens. It seems that you may be able to remove a softban by deleting the affected items or character and waiting for a certain amount of time. Could be false though. The information on this is unfortunately scarce and unreliable. 

TL;DR Back up your saves regularly, do not pick up items dropped by strangers and you might be ok playing online. Maybe. Hopefully.

Now as for the rest of the game, it is Dark Souls. Great game. My favorite since 2011. This time it comes with some changes such as the ability to rebind your jump button and holding up or down on the D pad to select your favorite spell/item. Neat.

The graphics have... changed? I've seen maybe 25% of this game so far and it is very very similiar. Hard to tell what is new, which is kind of a good thing I suppose. The differences that really stick out are the spell/fire/lightning effects which I actually think are quite pretty, so there is that. 

There is one visual change that is bothering me and that is the bonfire. Just as I said before "It goes from being iconic to generic and is actually lore breaking because it is supposed to be a magical flame." Most people playing the game today will just shrug at me like "why would you even care lol who cares what it looks like" because they just want to play online and slay bosses but I really value the artistic integrity of this game and to see crucial visual elements be tampered with in such an offhanded way just makes me feel sad inside. I think that if you remaster or remake a game you should keep the visuals as close to the original vision as possible.

Performance is solid for me. [spoiler] Blighttown finally running at 60fps [/spoiler] might be the highlight of this remaster so far. Looking at other reviews people seem to be having issues on certain configurations so I will recommend a bit of caution. No problems here though.

They changed matchmaking. Your weapon upgrade level now appears to be a factor. Doesn't really solve twinking (invading low levels) because you can still get overpowered unupgraded equipment and makes it more of a hassle to create planned midlevel invasion builds.

So, should you get this game? My view is that if you have not played Dark Souls, you should. It is one of the best games I have played. If you have a PS4, consider getting that version since it is much harder to cheat on that system. I won't be doing that because I can't justify paying full price + PS Plus for online. PC is fine though. Just back up your saves. In the event that you get softbanned you could still finish the game. For a veteran like myself though, even with the 50% discount on the PC version I find it to be a hard sell. What I wanted most of all from this game was a smoother running game with a revived online playerbase. Sure, I kinda got that. But what I also got were a bunch of unnecessary band-aid changes like the matchmaking and a tacked on anticheating system that punishes victims of cheating.

In essence, this remaster is fine. It should have been better. Dark Souls deserves better. If there was a sideways thumb rating then that is what I would have given it but there isn't. Because of the poor anticheat, adding inconveniences to matchmaking and tampering with the games original vision I will stick with my negative rating. I hope this helps you make an informed purchase decision. Have a good one.

[h1]Dark Souls: Demastered[/h1]

At this point, you've probably already heard that this is a bad remaster. I obviously agree since this is a negative review, though not for the same reasons given by many others. In fact, I can't believe that one of the most common criticisms is "the graphics look the same" when there's a significant difference in regards to the lighting and effects, unfortunately for the worse.

To begin with, a new lighting system has been implemented to make the game visually closer to Dark Souls III. The deep colors, bloom, and armor shine that are integral to Dark Souls' excellent art direction are now absent, and the overall visuals are excruciatingly flat and bland. While other miscellaneous effects are technically more detailed, they're often a bit excessive and aesthetically inferior. The slow, otherworldly flame of bonfires is now a generic fire, the screen effect when resting at a bonfire lacks transparency, bloodstains are strawberry jam, fog walls are too detailed and look flat from certain angles, the majestic glow of lava is severely downgraded, etc.

Sadly, there's examples of blatant ignorance of the artistic intent of the original throughout the entire "remaster", but the first of hundreds can be seen as soon as you finish creating a character. In the opening cutscene, the dim lighting of your prison cell was supposed to hide your character's hollow appearance before they move their head up to a small amount of light. The remaster ruins this reveal by increasing the brightness of the environment, making the protagonist's lifeless face immediately noticeable.

The visuals are indeed a big letdown regardless of whether you appreciate art or just want to see a lot of pixels and polygons, so the gameplay must be a letdown too, right? Well, if you want it to be like Roll Souls III, you'll be disappointed, but for those who simply want the pure Dark Souls experience, you'll be... much less disappointed. The gameplay is practically the same, though there's small changes here and there of varying quality. 

Starting with the good changes, you can use and offer multiple souls and Humanity at once, you can use the triggers to scroll through menus faster, and the password system is present and makes jolly cooperation with friends easier. That's about it; the rest are either bizarre or outright dumb. 

I personally liked how world hosts had to use their own Estus to heal phantoms, but I understand why the devs made it so phantoms can now use Estus. That said, I dislike how you get more Estus usage whenever an enemy phantom is defeated; it just makes gank squads way worse. Speaking of gank squads, the Dried Finger item works exactly like DS3's, allowing for a third phantom and a second phantom invader. On the bright side, at least invasions don't prioritize gankers.

Another pair of gameplay tweaks are related to bonfires. First of all, you can now swap your covenant alignment at any bonfire. While there's still consequences for covenant abandonment, the encouragement of swapping between them willy-nilly ruins the feeling of permanence they once had. A new bonfire has also been added next to Vamos, which is a ridiculous addition that undermines how the world of Lordran is designed and serves as a beginners trap for brave adventurers that choose to venture into the Catacombs before obtaining the Lordvessel.

Honestly, I could go on and on and talk about what is and isn't different, but I've already gone over most of the noteworthy alterations. However, one of the strangest modifications that nobody talks about is the sound. Though I can't really tell if the audio quality is improved, I have noticed that there are sounds that have been slightly changed, the sound of bonfire warping being one of the few to come to mind. Also, the Blighttown bell now rings in the worlds of other players when rung, which is a neat addition, but hilariously enough the devs dun goofed and used the Undead Parish bell sound.

That alone summarizes the competency of Dark Souls: Remastered. QLOC, the developer of the remaster, wanted to make a bunch of minor enhancements, yet almost every single one of those minor enhancements ended up being a mistake, and they all piled up to make DS:R an inferior experience. I would recommend buying the original Dark Souls PtDE instead for those that don't own it, but for some asinine reason Bamco removed it from the Steam Store despite it being a perfectly functional product even without the fan-made DSFix mod. Because of that, I have no choice but to recommend Dark Souls: Remastered to those that haven't played it, because it's still one of the best video games ever made. But for those that already played the original release, which I assume is the majority of people that would even buy the remaster given how much the original PtDE sold, stay away. Not only is it ludicrous to pay for a game you already have on the same gaming platform, it's the worst way to replay this masterpiece.

This game means a lot to me. Booting up DS1 and going back to Lordran always feels like coming back home.

Foreword: The Remastered edition has a handful of quality of life fixes to the game that make it easy to recommend to someone (namely functional online with no strings attached). IMO, if you're just looking to play Dark Souls, look no further.

Dark Souls is, more than likely, the best game you’ll ever play – and a mandatory game for anyone who’s capable of picking up a controller to play through.

First, to clear up a strong misconception about the game: Dark Souls is not hard, and it’s definitely not so hard only "hardcore gamers" can beat it, Dark Souls is “choose your own difficulty” in the strictest sense.

The game has a hundred ways for you to tune its difficulty, and 99% of the complaints about difficulty come from people hearing about the difficulty, going a harder way at the beginning and saying “oh man I guess this is just too tough for me”, or stubbornly refusing to make any concessions and paying the price.

In example: the two friends I have who’ve given up on Dark Souls (for the time being) gave up because they chose a very newbie-unfriendly way to play the game, then said to themselves “Oh, this is too hard, I just can’t do it”. 

One decided he wanted to do a playthrough using only shields for weapons(!). Not exactly the easiest start to any action RPG, and Dark Souls is no different. Didn't want to adjust after the first boss; gave up on the game altogether.

The other friend chose a starting class she liked the idea of (backstabbing thief), then refused to adjust her character to her playstyle after she got frustrated that she wasn't dealing the damage any other weapon does outside of backstabbing and status effects, leading to a massive drought in progression and eventually halting it altogether. Never even tried another weapon.

That isn’t to say that you CAN’T beat the game with a buckler or a dagger – you can, I’ve done it, thousands of people have done it. It just tunes the game’s difficulty beyond what the average person is expecting or is capable of dealing with, and that’s where people go wrong with Dark Souls.

You having trouble with dodging? Pick up a shield. Getting your shield knocked around? Pick up a greatshield. Struggling on that fire damage boss and it’s driving you crazy? Put on some fire resistant armor. Gang of thieves cornering you? Try some heavier armor to resist getting stunlocked. Snakes firing lightning bolts at you from 500 feet away while you’re going through a deathmaze? Take out a bow and shoot them.

Dark Souls is pure insanity with how many options there are. There isn't one answer to any one problem, there are hundreds. If you're feeling trapped, widen your horizon a bit.

It isn’t all the player’s fault, mind you. A handful of important events and techniques are never properly described to the player, and that’d be a primary critique I have of Dark Souls – any of them. 

Most of the game’s standard playthrough difficulty (aside from people needing to get used to picking up a bow when that skeleton archer has pelted them one too many times, or taking off their starting gear to slap on the pyromancer set against Quelaag) comes from the tutorial area and the upgrade system.

The tutorial area sets you against a boss with just your fists – you deal TWO damage to it per hit, and to do the fight with just fists would take roughly *20 minutes* of perfect gameplay. 

Obviously, you aren’t expected to be perfect against the first real enemy you encounter for 20 minutes, but since the game has a public view of being “impossibly difficult” most people just assume they are. And when they can’t, they quit, and therein lies the “game is too hard” stroke the community constantly has.

You can just listen to the orange sign on the ground saying "run", walk past the giant 825 HP demon instead of trying to punch it to death with your fists, and the game will lock the door behind you. It’ll give you some of the gear you chose at the beginning, and then it’ll send you back in with him once your armed. You can equip all of that gear, do a plunging attack down on the boss for a quarter of its health, and THAT is Dark Souls difficulty. 

It gives you all the tools you need to beat anything – but it’s up to you whether you use them, or if you'll just sit the top of the ledge not reading a singular sign and then getting cleaved in a half when the demon dunks you.

As for Firelink Shrine (the hub area), you can go three different ways – down to New Londo with the invincible ghosts, or over to the cemetery with the ever-resurrecting skeletons, or up to the aquaduct with the normal enemies that die in 2-3 hits and stay dead. I bet you can guess where you’re supposed to go with the knowledge that the game isn’t built to be impossible.

And hey, on Taurus Demon, turn your butt around when you come out of the fog gate and go up the ladder. Wham, Archers handled.

Lastly, after said Taurus Demon, there'll be a BIG bridge. Hug the right, and sprint till you hit a divot in the right fence of the bridge. It's a safe spot, and takes you down to a bonfire (after you kick a ladder). Safety.

That's it for stupid tutorial stuff that needs better explaining than the game will give you.

The upgrade system: it’s not an overtly accessible system until you’ve hit the wiki, and you CAN’T hit the wiki until you’ve beaten the game unless you want to spoil the living hell out of yourself, which let me reassure you: you don’t want to do that, for this game or any of the FromSoftware RPGs. It's one of the only ways to majorly sully your experience.

Basically, when you’ve found a weapon that you know you like (preferably one you think is busted or broken in some capacity, since that will allow you to abuse what you think is so strong about it better), you take it to a blacksmith and upgrade the snot out of it. 

Simple enough as long as you know the system exists (a lot of people walk right past it or kill the blacksmith because “haha this game lets you kill NPCs”), but the biggest problem is that the system can be expanded (for the majority of the playerbase) twice. 

You can pick up Embers that give the Blacksmith the ability to empower your weapon even more, and since most people never pick these up, they play the whole game at 1/3rd the power level they could be (at most). 

I HEAVILY recommend AGAINST using youtube to guide you through any portion of the game, or guides in general, as they spoil you heavily and rob you of your Dark Souls experience, but I would make an exception for this if you’ve upgraded your weapon to +5 and feel like you’re due for an upgrade.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dEWmlY4HCI0 for the first ember (+5 to +10)
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=plw7kuCDTf8 for the second ember (+10 to +15)

I would avoid looking at the comments, recommendations on the side, etc, as any Dark Souls search on youtube will inevitably lead to a hundred spoilers, and all of them are worth seeing for yourself unspoiled.

Most of this review was spent on making sure people reading knew that the game was not some impossible wall, but rather a “choose your own difficulty” style game with some poor tutorials, but to round out the review with some other must-mentions:

Dark Souls is an outstanding game that manages to capture the feel of a Metroidvania in a 3D space. Though most renowned for its "difficulty", the game is also rightfully known for its incredible world-building, stunning environments, and surprisingly robust character-building. 

In truth, the game is not so much difficult as it is challenging. The first challenge is in growing accustomed to the game's controls, which at first feel clunky and unresponsive until you realize just how fluid they allow you to be, and that the clunkiness was merely your own clumsiness at controlling your character. Additionally, challenging enemies and boss fights may at first seem overwhelming, but the game always seems to know exactly how far it can push you, and overcoming even the earliest challenges end up feeling like great accomplishments as a result. 

The game rewards both exploration and caution, but most of all, it rewards perseverance. In short, Dark Souls earns its reputation, and is a game well worth playing.

Dark Souls is likely the game that had the largest impact on me as an adult, and truly helped me mature into the person I am today. Bloodborne was my first Fromsoft game, but Dark Souls was the first Fromsoft game where I'd say I actually had the full experience. I distinctly remember going into the game knowing about its reputation as a difficult game, going to the graveyard outside Firelink, fighting the skeletons, and thinking, "Huh, these guys are tough. Oh well, this must just be how the game is." I then proceeded to go down to Vamos's bonfire and get stuck for multiple hours in the bonewheel pit trying to get back out of the Catacombs. It was a spiritual experience. Another memory of mine was fighting Gaping Dragon for the first time, where I managed to kill it on my first try. I was so incredibly thrilled I managed to do it on my first attempt, and while it might seem silly in retrospect, it is a memory I will always hold close to my heart. Fast forward to the end of the game, and I was somehow still not aware of weight thresholds and roll types. I was fighting Gwyn with full Stone Knight amor, Black Knight sword, and fatrolling everywhere. After many attempts I suddenly came to the realization that there was in fact different dodges bases on the weight of your character and equipped the Gold-Hemmed Black set with a Reinforced Club and proceeded to beat him using that. Since then, I've replayed Dark Souls so many times I've honestly lost count. After playing the Souls series solo for years, I managed to get a friend to play with me, and despite it being her first rpg, she stuck it out all the way to the end. Today, it is a tradition of ours to take friends of ours new and old and guide them through the entire series as a kind of bonding experience. I think at this point we've played the series with upwards of twelve people, and I don't intend to let that stop any time soon. To review the game more critically, it's moment to moment gameplay can feel kind of floaty compared to later entries in the series, however where the game truly excels is in its interconnected world design and layout. If you know where to go and what to do, the game truly opens up, leaving you free to explore the areas out of "order". You can easily beat the game in thirteen bosses, and even less if you're acquainted with some of the easy skips and glitches. The bossing experience is rather easy in this game, at least compared to the rest of the series, however that does not make it any less satisfying to go through and experience them on repeat playthroughs. Dark Souls also shines in its build variety and weapon diversity. Having upwards of one hundred different weapons and extremely customizable upgrade paths, every playthrough will find a way to be unique. There are also many obscure and niche mechanics that not many players will interact with outside of those who truly dedicate themselves to the game. Things like Gravelording and Miracle Resonance are not likely to be interacted with by most players, but for veterans they act as ways to diversify and enjoy playthroughs after hundreds of hours of playtime. Unfortunately, Dark Souls NPC quest design is not very friendly to newcomers to the series, and I believe this to be one of its biggest flaws. There are many interesting characters that are a really strong addition to the game, but most players are unlikely to finish their questlines as you often have to go way out of your way to explore and re-explore areas to find every quest stage for most NPCS. Another "flaw" of Dark Souls is that the second half of the game does not quite live up to the first half. While I have learned to love it, I can see why many people take issue with it, as places like Lost Izalith and the Crystal Cave are not as polished as areas like Undead Burg and Anor Londo. Dark Souls remains my favorite Souls game, and I will always encourage people to play it.

A pretty bare bones HD retexture of the original.  Includes a couple of conveniences like using multiple consumables at a time, a new bonfire near a merchant NPC, and being able to switch covenants on at checkpoints.

However, for the major overhauls, there's something to negate the change almost immediately.  More players and better connectivity for PvP and Co-Op, but the match making is based off level-adjustments from powerful items in your inventory you can get by random chance and might not even have currently in use, making it easy to abuse by invaders and unfair to newcomers.  The ability to use your Estus Flask even as an invader or summon, but now everyone can spam healing AND you can still carry mushrooms, divine blessings and humanity in stacks of 99 as alternative healing sources.  Various bug fixes like dead-angling and ghost hits, but chain backstabs is still a problem.  Move swapping and item menu duplication patched, but perfect frame duplication and tumble buffing still exists.

Really, for any previous PC Prepare to Die Edition users, this won't be worth the money you spend on it.  There's nothing really here to gain and some of the changes I find a bit detrimental to the game play and visuals (like Elite Knight armor being dull looking now).  For console, this is the big patch you've been waiting for without DSFix available to you.  However, I very much can't recommend this game because of the terrible idea of removing the original Prepare to Die Edition for purchase entirely.  That's just a low, greedy move NamcoBandai.

2024 Review from a person who has not played any of the actual Dark Souls games, but has completed all of Elden Ring and Sekiro.  I finished this one after 37 hours, taking my time.

The graphics are a bit dated and the mechanics are a little clunky, but the game holds up.  The way the map is structured is amazing.  All of the levels loop around and into each other, so even though you don't get fast travel until fairly deep in the game it does not drag.  I did have to look up a map though from time to time as there is not one in the game and I didn't memorize all of that.  From a pure "tracing back to the roots of what this type of game is" perspective this one is worth playing.  I did play it on the steam deck for a decent portion of the time.

As for difficulty, I was surprised to discover that it was sort of easy.  I have completed Elden Ring + DLC and Sekrio so it may just be that I  have "got gud".  The combat is slower paced than those games but more deliberate.  If you press to swing your sword twice you better have meant it, because it is swinging twice.  The difficulty in this game was not really in the bosses in my opinion, but in the runbacks and the level parkour.  More of that later.

One of the things that does not get talked about much is the game's sense of humor.  Its the baked in little things, like only Rats have humanity.  For example, One of the first bosses in the game is fought on top of a rather narrow wall.  While fighting him, I turned him so that his back was to the edge.  When he jumped away from me, he jumped off the wall to his death; Victory Achieved.  Hilarious.  Other times the game pranks you, saying "You thought one gargoyle was the boss?  How about 2?"  And every character in the game is a terrible person with gallows humor (except for Solaire, he's the best), while some of the monsters are kind of chill.  There were literal times that I laughed out loud at the game and that does not get talked about much.

What I did not enjoy was some of the more dated level traversal aspects.  Like Instant death or just a big waste of time associated with falling from a higher place.  Getting knocked off that higher place happens.  Also, there is no jump button; you have to be running and the press the run button again to do a jump.  In some places this is required.  Heck in the Bed of Chaos boss fight it is required over instant death pits.  Also, rolling and running while locked on is limited.  And some of the achievements are literally RNG based.  Overall I felt like this game was worth playing and finishing, but not something I'm going to be chasing everything in.

It took me 10 years to finish the Prepare to Die Edition. Back in 2014, I abruptly stopped at Gwyn's fog gate and never managed to complete the fight. Now, in 2024, I got pulled back in with the Remastered version.

This game is a gem. While players often associate Dark Souls with its difficulty and jank, in reality, the game is deep—almost poetic. Aiming for 100% achievements requires you to play the game 2.5 times, giving you plenty of time to absorb the untold lore and feel the weight of the world, the setting, and the struggle.

The final boss, Gwyn, is often depicted as an easy or meme-worthy fight, but it’s much more than that. The battle itself feels intimate, almost melancholic, with the haunting piano melody of Gwyn, Lord of Cinder underscoring the fight. Interestingly, the melody is played only on the white keys of the piano, symbolizing Gwyn's desperate avoidance of the darkness he fears. It’s not a triumphant showdown but a sobering confrontation with a god clinging to the remnants of his power and purpose. Gwyn’s aggressive, relentless attacks convey desperation more than dominance, as though he’s fighting not just you but the inevitable passage of time.

Dark Souls is a masterpiece that transcends its reputation, weaving a narrative of solitude, agony, and survival into every aspect of its design.

It was fairly surprising when FromSoftware announced that they were remastering Dark Souls in 2018. Sure, at that time the game was a modest 7 years old, and we're currently living in an era where remastering previous remasters is a thing. However, many fans of the series would've rather seen some effort put into bringing Demon's Souls to PC, or at the very least remastering that release instead, which is now a decade old, for modern consoles. Instead, fans received one of the most half-baked attempts at a remaster in recent history.

It's fair to say that the original Dark Souls PC port had some pretty hefty problems; a 30 FPS cap, low resolutions, crashing, and not to mention the infamous optimization problems in Blighttown. After it was apparent that no official patch would swoop in to fix these fairly large grievances, the gaming community stepped in to fix FromSoftware's blatant oversights. Thankfully, most of these concerns have been addressed in Dark Souls: Remastered. In my complete playthrough, I didn't experience a single crash, and on my GTX 1080/i7-6700k rig I only experienced weird frame drops in a couple areas. The latter only happened for a few seconds in perhaps 3-4 locations, and none of those were Blighttown. The game can also now run up to a 4k resolution natively, rather than relying on any patched-in fixes.

That's about where it ends for what's good about Dark Souls: Remastered. To say that this "remaster" is lazy is actually pretty forgiving. There's excruciatingly little difference in the visuals between this release and the original, and somehow the upgraded lighting just feels polished and out of place in an otherwise dark and gritty game. These "upgrades" actually detract from the vibe and atmosphere of the original, bringing with it some kind of spit n' shine that has scrubbed out the grit and grime of the older textures. Overall, it just looks far too bright and clean for a Souls game, and because of that it loses a ton of its gothic allure. The audio doesn't come across as "remastered" at all, either. Using a 7.1 surround sound headset, I was unable to hear any difference in the soundtrack, ambience, or sound effects.

There's not really a lot more to say about Dark Souls: Remastered. It's a total waste of time on the part of the developer, and a total waste of money on the part of the consumer. Everything included in this release, including graphic upgrades, is available as free mods in the Prepare to Die Edition. However, it's impossible to not recommend this release since Bandai Namco pulled Dark Souls: Prepare to Die Edition from sale on Steam. Only buy this "remaster" if you haven't experienced Dark Souls and you have no way of obtaining the original edition instead. Those who owned the original edition of the game received a 50% discount for the Remastered version, but even $25 is too steep to pay for this slap in the face. I ended up grabbing it on sale for around $12, and I still feel ripped off.
